summary: The most probable root cause is the pricing-engine config change cfg-3120, which at 2026-05-20T12:04:16Z ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100, forcing all quote traffic onto the compute-heavy GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator path (20000 paths, 6465ms observed) — a ~40x p99 jump on pricing-engine that then trips order-service's 2500ms quote timeout. This is supported by a consistent causal chain of verified observations: the flag flip is the only change in the ~5 minutes before the first slow calc (F14), the first GreeksV2 slow-calc log immediately follows it (F7), pricing-engine p99 was flat until that bucket (F9), pricing-engine's own errors name calculator=GreeksV2 exceeding its 2000ms budget (F12), and order-service timeouts begin after the pricing-engine latency jump (F8, F11). Confidence is medium (0.60) rather than high: no canary latency history for the GreeksV2 path and no resource metrics were obtained, and the reporter's suspected market-data-service protobuf deploy (dep-6111) is plausible but contradicted by that service being healthy and not the earliest-affected component (F10). Mitigation should be to roll the flag back and verify pricing-engine p99 recovers.

ranked_hypotheses.title: GreeksV2 flag ramp (cfg-3120) made an expensive calculator serve all traffic, saturating pricing-engine
ranked_hypotheses.statement: At 12:04:16Z cfg-3120 ramped flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100, moving all pricing-engine quote traffic onto the GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator code path. That path is compute-heavy (20000 Monte-Carlo paths, 6465ms observed) and exceeds the 2000ms internal deadline, driving pricing-engine p99 from ~60ms to ~2500ms and its 'request deadline exceeded ... calculator=GreeksV2' errors. order-service, which calls pricing-engine over http with a 2500ms timeout, then fails the quote step.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5 -> 100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:16Z, sending all quote traffic through the GreeksV2 path
GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator is compute-heavy and slow: 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took 6465ms' first at 12:05:21Z, ~65s after the flag flip
pricing-engine p99 jumps from flat ~58-62ms to ~2489ms in the 12:05:00Z bucket and stays elevated through 13:56Z
pricing-engine emits 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' from 12:06:41Z
order-service quote calls to pricing-engine exceed the 2500ms downstream threshold, producing 225 'pricing-engine quote call timed out' errors starting 12:06:10Z
order-service error_rate jumps from ~0.2% baseline to 6-8.4% in the bucket starting 12:04:00Z

assumptions: The GreeksV2 path was not already slow at 5% traffic (no canary latency history for cfg-3120 was obtained) — if it was, blame shifts from the ramp to the code path itself
No untracked pricing-engine deploy occurred near onset; deployment queries found none (F13)
No resource-saturation metrics were captured, so a coincident CPU/memory fault cannot be formally excluded

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service protobuf deploy dep-6111 (reporter's suspicion) broke quote payloads downstream
ranked_hypotheses.statement: At 11:56:45Z market-data-service shipped dep-6111 v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf'. The protobuf payloads are valid but incompatible with what pricing-engine (or an intermediate consumer) can parse, so pricing-engine wastes time on parse retries/fallbacks, inflating its latency and eventually causing order-service quote timeouts.

causal_chain.claim: dep-6111 (market-data-service v5.2.0, protobuf quote serialization) deploys at 11:56:45Z, the only deployment in the window
pricing-engine fetches quotes from market-data-service over http and would be the consumer of the new protobuf payloads
protobuf payload incompatibility causes downstream parse retries/fallbacks in pricing-engine, inflating latency
inflated pricing-engine latency pushes quote calls past order-service's 2500ms timeout, producing quote timeouts

assumptions: The protobuf change produced payloads that pricing-engine cannot fully parse (untested)
Any parse cost would have to account for a ~40x p99 jump on its own

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache fault degraded independently, propagating to pricing-engine and market-data-service
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A shared dependency of pricing-engine and market-data-service — redis-cache (the only shared component besides the direct http edge) — degraded at ~12:04-12:05Z, causing cache-miss storms/retries that inflated pricing-engine latency and eventually order-service quote timeouts, independently of both the protobuf deploy and the flag ramp.

causal_chain.claim: redis-cache is the only shared component linking pricing-engine and market-data-service, and is shared=true
redis-cache degrades (failover/empty replica/eviction) at onset, causing a cold-cache miss storm
cache misses inflate pricing-engine quote computation latency to ~2.5s
order-service quote calls to pricing-engine exceed 2500ms and time out

assumptions: An untracked redis-cache event (no config/deploy record) occurred at onset
The error signature would look like cache misses rather than the observed GreeksV2 deadline-exceeded messages

ranked_hypotheses.title: Resource saturation (CPU/memory/thread-pool) on pricing-engine or order-service
ranked_hypotheses.statement: pricing-engine or order-service hit CPU/memory/GC/connection-pool saturation around 12:04Z, causing the latency spike and timeouts; the flag ramp and protobuf deploy are coincidental. Structurally resembles HIST-113 (pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open).

causal_chain.claim: pricing-engine CPU/memory or thread pool saturates near 12:04Z
saturation inflates quote computation latency to ~2.5s
order-service quote calls exceed 2500ms and time out

assumptions: Resource metrics would show saturation (unqueried — budget exhausted)
The compute-heavy GreeksV2 path is not itself sufficient to explain the latency

facts.statement: cfg-3120 changed pricing-engine key flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5 to 100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:16Z, authored by pm-experiments, and was the only change in the 11:40–12:10Z window.

The first pricing-engine slow-calc log, 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took 6465ms', occurred at 2026-05-20T12:05:21Z, immediately preceded by the cfg-3120 config application at 12:04:16Z.

pricing-engine p99 was flat ~58–62ms through the 11:56–11:59 buckets, then jumped to ~2489ms in the bucket starting 12:05:00Z and stayed ~2500–2850ms through 13:56Z — a new regression, not pre-existing.

pricing-engine's error signature is 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' (276 occurrences, first at 12:06:41Z), i.e. the GreeksV2 calculator exceeds its internal budget.
order-service quote timeouts begin at 2026-05-20T12:06:10Z, after pricing-engine's first slow calc at 12:05:21Z, with 225 ERROR lines of 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after <n>ms'.
order-service error_rate jumped from a ~0.17–0.25% baseline to 6.08% in the bucket starting 12:04:00Z and ~8.1–8.4% thereafter.

Only one deployment occurred across all services in 10:00–13:59Z: dep-6111, market-data-service v5.2.0, at 11:56:00Z ('Switch quote serialization to protobuf'), status live, not rolled back; a pricing-engine-scoped deploy query for 11:30–12:06:30Z returned zero.
market-data-service shows no errors after dep-6111 and stayed responsive ('served batch of requests, p50=393ms' at 12:01:29Z); it is not the earliest-affected component.
order-service reaches market-data-service only indirectly via pricing-engine (http); pricing-engine and market-data-service both hold 'cache' edges to redis-cache, flagged shared=true.
Config-change queries scoped to redis-cache and market-data-service for 11:00–13:59Z each returned count 0; no tracked change landed on the shared cache or market-data-service around onset.

Historical precedents do not match a serialization change; HIST-107 (redis cold-cache storm) and HIST-113 (pricing-engine CPU saturation) implicate redis-cache or pricing-engine capacity, and HIST-101 (bcrypt cost config change) structurally resembles a flag ramp making an expensive code path serve all traffic.

assumptions: The GreeksV2 code path was not already slow at 5% traffic before cfg-3120: no canary latency history for the flag was obtained, so if it was already slow the blame shifts from the ramp to the code path itself.
No untracked pricing-engine deploy occurred near onset: deployment queries found none, but 'no deploy record' is not the same as 'no deploy occurred'.
No resource-saturation fault (CPU/memory/GC/thread-pool) or shared redis-cache fault occurred at onset: no resource or cache metrics were captured, so a coincident fault cannot be formally excluded.

order-service's 2500ms pricing-engine timeout and pricing-engine's 2000ms internal deadline are as stated in the observation findings and are the mechanism transferring pricing-engine latency to order-service quote failures.
The deployment and config record set returned by the tools is complete for the window, modulo the noted partial config-audit shard 2/3.

timeline.event: Only deployment in the window: dep-6111, market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' by v.rao, status live (not rolled back).
market-data-service post-deploy shows no errors and stays responsive ('served batch of requests, p50=393ms').

recommended_actions.action: Roll back cfg-3120: set pricing-engine flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct back from 100 to 5 (or 0) to remove the GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo path from the bulk of quote traffic.
recommended_actions.rationale: cfg-3120 is the only change in the ~5 minutes before the first slow calc and directly alters the calculator named in pricing-engine's slow-calc log and deadline-exceeded errors; reverting it is the fastest way to restore pricing-engine p99 and order-service quote success.

recommended_actions.action: Confirm recovery after rollback: watch pricing-engine p99 return toward the ~58–62ms baseline and order-service error_rate return to ~0.2% and quote timeouts cease.
recommended_actions.rationale: Pre-change baselines are known (p99 ~60ms; order-service error_rate ~0.17–0.25%), giving clear success criteria to verify the mitigation rather than assume it.

recommended_actions.action: If the flag cannot be rolled back quickly, mitigate at the boundary: raise order-service's pricing-engine call timeout (currently 2500ms) and/or shed load, but treat this only as a stopgap since it does not fix the underlying 6465ms compute cost.
recommended_actions.rationale: order-service fails because its 2500ms timeout is exceeded by pricing-engine's 2000ms-budget breach and ~2.5s p99; raising the timeout may reduce failures but will not address the saturated GreeksV2 path.

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back dep-6111 (market-data-service protobuf v5.2.0) as the first action; if rollback risk is low and cheap, it may be tested only after the flag rollback to discriminate H2, since market-data-service is healthy and not the earliest-affected component.
recommended_actions.rationale: The protobuf deploy is the reporter's suspicion but is contradicted by market-data-service showing no errors and staying responsive, and by order-service reaching it only through pricing-engine; rolling it back first risks churn without evidence.

recommended_actions.action: Establish canary latency history / SLO gating for the GreeksV2 path before any future ramp, and cap rollout_pct increases behind latency thresholds.
recommended_actions.rationale: The ramp moved 100% of traffic onto a path never validated for production-scale latency; a canary history would have caught the ~40x p99 jump at 5% and prevented the all-traffic ramp.

recommended_actions.action: Capture pricing-engine CPU/memory/GC/thread-pool metrics (and redis-cache miss/latency) around 12:04–12:06Z in a follow-up to close the H3/H4 resource-saturation and shared-cache questions.
recommended_actions.rationale: No resource or cache telemetry was obtained; confirming the GreeksV2 compute path (rather than generic CPU saturation or a redis-cache fault) is the sole cause strengthens the conclusion and rules out the remaining hypotheses.

data_gaps: No resource/telemetry metrics (CPU, memory, GC, connection/thread-pool) were captured for pricing-engine or order-service (query_metrics returned 'budget_exhausted'), so H4 resource saturation cannot be confirmed or excluded.
No redis-cache telemetry (miss rate, evictions, latency, connection saturation) was queried, so H3 shared-cache fault rests only on topology, with no supporting data.
Blast radius to other services calling pricing-engine or market-data-service was not checked, so the full impact scope is unestablished.
No canary/rollout history for cfg-3120 at 5% traffic, so it is unknown whether the GreeksV2 path was already slow before the 100% ramp.
The first get_config_changes call (tc-005) was partial ('config-audit shard 2/3 did not respond'); residual risk that a config change on order-service or market-data-service is unlisted.
No query for untracked cluster/infra events (node restarts, autoscaling, maintenance) that could have contributed without a change record.
market-data-service's edge to exchange-gateway and the external exchange-api (has_telemetry=false) was not evaluated for latency contribution.
No precedent specific to a protobuf/serialization change breaking downstream callers was found (historical search budget not exhausted before tool limits).
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Tracing the onset to 11:56Z (the dep-6111 deploy) rather than 12:04–12:05Z would shift support toward H2 (market-data-service protobuf).

Metrics showing the GreeksV2 path was already slow at 5% traffic before cfg-3120 would move blame from the ramp to the code path itself (a property of the GreeksV2 implementation rather than the rollout).
Evidence of CPU/memory/GC/thread-pool saturation on pricing-engine independent of the GreeksV2 compute cost would support H4 (resource saturation) over H1.
Cache-miss/latency/eviction anomalies on redis-cache at ~12:04–12:06Z (with no corresponding config/deploy change) would support H3 (shared-cache fault).
Failure of pricing-engine p99 and order-service errors to recover after rolling back cfg-3120 would falsify H1 as the sufficient cause and redirect to H2/H3/H4.
Discovery of an additional unlisted config or deploy change (e.g. from config-audit shard 2/3) affecting pricing-engine or order-service around onset would re-open the causal attribution.

findings.statement: Only one deployment in 10:00–13:59Z across ALL services: dep-6111, market-data-service v5.2.0, deployed 2026-05-20T11:56:00Z by v.rao, 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' ('protobuf quote payloads for internal callers'), status 'live', rolled_back_at null. No deployment on order-service, pricing-engine, or any other service in the window.

Two config changes in the window (full, non-partial retry): cfg-3118 api-gateway 'ratelimit.burst' 200→250 at 2026-05-20T10:30:00Z (config-bot), and cfg-3120 pricing-engine 'flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct' 5→100 at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z by 'pm-experiments' ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic'). The pricing-engine flag ramp at 12:04Z is ~8 minutes after the protobuf deploy.

order-service's quote path (dependency edges, caller→callee) is: api-gateway → order-service → {pricing-engine (http), ledger-db (db), exchange-gateway (http), kafka (queue-produce)}; pricing-engine → {market-data-service (http), redis-cache (cache)}. So order-service does NOT call market-data-service directly — it goes through pricing-engine. market-data-service → redis-cache (cache) and → exchange-gateway (http).

redis-cache is the only shared component connecting pricing-engine and market-data-service: both have edges to redis-cache (kind 'cache'), and redis-cache is flagged shared=true, owner platform. So a shared cache is a possible cross-service path from the market-data serialization change to pricing-engine latency, independent of the direct pricing-engine→market-data-service http edge.

Other shared platform components in the graph: ledger-db (postgres, shared=true, used by order-service) and kafka (kafka, shared=true, order-service produces to it). These — plus redis-cache — are shared components that could transmit faults from a neighbour into order-service or pricing-engine.

Historical leads (search 'quote timeout serialization change'): HIST-107 (2025-12-09) 'Cold cache storm after redis failover', services redis-cache + market-data-service, symptoms cache miss storm / quote latency, root cause 'Redis primary failure promoted an empty replica', resolution warmed cache + fixed replica sync checks; and HIST-113 (2026-01-28) 'pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open', symptom quote timeouts + cpu 99%, root cause capacity saturation, resolution raised replica count. Both are leads only, not evidence about the current incident; note neither prior incident was caused by a serialization/deploy change, and both implicate redis-cache or pricing-engine capacity rather than market-data's protobuf change.

findings.statement: Full re-query of deployments 10:00–13:59Z across all services returned exactly one: dep-6111 market-data-service v5.2.0 at 11:56:00Z, status live, rolled_back_at null. A second, narrower query scoped to service=pricing-engine for 11:30–12:06:30Z returned count 0 deployments, so nothing was deployed to pricing-engine (or its own stack) near the 12:05 onset.

A tight-window config query (11:40–12:10Z) returned exactly one change: cfg-3120, pricing-engine, key flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct old_value 5 → new_value 100, changed_at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z, author pm-experiments, 'Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic'. This is the only change in the ~5 minutes before the 12:05:21Z first slow calc, and it directly alters the pricing-engine calculator named in the slow-calc log.

Dependency re-query confirms order-service reaches market-data-service only indirectly: order-service → pricing-engine (http) → market-data-service (http). market-data-service and pricing-engine both have edges to redis-cache (kind 'cache'), and redis-cache is flagged type 'redis', owner platform, shared=true. So redis-cache is the single shared component (other than the direct http edge) through which market-data-service could affect pricing-engine.

config-change queries scoped to redis-cache and to market-data-service for 11:00–13:59Z each returned count 0: no config change touched the shared cache or market-data-service in the window. Hence no tracked change landed on the shared dependency (redis-cache) of pricing-engine at any point around onset.

redis-cache is shared by a wider set than pricing-engine/market-data-service: auth-service and portfolio-service also have cache edges to it, and api-gateway and portfolio-service call market-data-service over http. If the shared cache were the fault vector, those extra callers are additional exposed neighbours that were not checked in this task.

Historical precedent search gives mixed leads, none matching a serialization change: HIST-107 (2025-12-09) red-cache/market-data-service cold-cache storm (redis primary failure promoted an empty replica) and two bad_deployment precedents HIST-101 (bcrypt cost 10→14) and HIST-109 (JWT clock-skew default) where a config/code value change released at rollout caused the latency — the latter pattern (HIST-101) structurally resembles a flag ramp that makes an expensive code path serve all traffic.
